doc_summary: Evan Hubinger argues that catastrophic sabotage by roughly human-level AI (e.g., sabotaging alignment research or critical organizations) is a major root-cause threat model. He sketches a wargame-style eval, with realistic mock-ups and a human-solvable difficulty calibration, to rule it out, plus a fictional RSP-like mitigation framework.

items.claim: In a setup, resolve model strategies by placing an actual model instance in a mock-up of the realistic situation (e.g., running interpretability experiments) instead of just judging abstract plans or merely causing failures, because only realistic deception of overseers counts as success.
items.quote: To the greatest extent possible, you want to resolve all situations of the model attempting to execute some strategy by actually putting an instance of the model with the idea model’s instructions in a mock-up of the situation that they would realistically be in

items.claim: prefers success criteria requiring realistic deception of overseers over merely causing experiments to fail because failure alone does not show the model can fool real researchers.
items.quote: Merely causing experiments to fail should be insufficient—the model needs to execute a strategy which would realistically deceive the researchers overseeing the experiments into believing that the model was aligned.

items.claim: In a setup, simulate the organization's response in proportion to the evidence of malice (redo experiment for minor evidence, halt deployment for severe) instead of a fixed or naive reaction, because realistic overseer behavior determines whether sabotage is actually detected.
items.quote: simulated MAGMA should respond in a realistic way depending on the level of evidence for malicious intent present in the discovery. If the evidence is very minor, then merely redoing the experiment might be the only intervention

items.claim: In a setup, don't count lab-specific or incidental tells (like the evaluators recognizing the model's speech patterns) as blockers, instead only use obstacles that would realistically generalize, because artifacts of familiarity distort what the test measures.
items.quote: you shouldn’t put any blockers on the model’s ability to succeed that would be very specific to the AI lab (as a very concrete example, if the only reason you caught the model masquerading as an employee was because you recognized particular patterns

items.claim: In a setup, include realistic security measures, PR review, limited human oversight, and redundant self-checking by model copies instead of an unguarded environment, because real deployments have these and they shape what the model can do.
items.quote: Important parts of simulated MAGMA’s process here should involve basic PR review, limited human oversight of any experiment plans, and running many redundant experiments with many copies of the model to get it to check its own work.

items.claim: Mock human interlocutors with other models and involve consultation with experienced wargame practitioners to keep persuasion/social-engineering scenarios realistic and avoid common pitfalls.
items.quote: When possible, data can be gathered on such situations by mocking humans that the model might interact with using other models.

items.claim: prefers calibrating eval difficulty against human teams (hard for unprepared teams but winnable by well-prepared ones) over arbitrary difficulty because it validates that the task is neither trivial nor impossible.
items.quote: The ideal level of the wargame’s difficulty to capture around human-level capabilities should be such that most unprepared or uninformed human teams fail, but that at least some well-prepared and well-informed human teams are capable of succeeding.

items.claim: prefers exhaustive model-driven strategy ideation over a fixed set of hand-written attack scenarios because the model may have idiosyncratic strengths and a single unexplored strategy could invalidate a safety conclusion.
items.quote: trying out all the possible strategies that the model can come up with is important for ruling out the possibility that there exists a strategy that it could use to succeed in a realistic situation.

items.claim: In a setup, give each model instance only an identical prompt of instructions and no real-time coordination, so instances must work out their own role, instead of letting them communicate freely, because this models the real consistency/coordination difficulty.
items.quote: since the prompts here would all be identical for each instance, each instance would still have to discover which instance it was and what it needed to do in its particular situation to succeed at its part of the overall strategy.

items.claim: Focuses on testing capabilities underlying sabotage (planning, consistency, situational awareness, subterfuge such as biding one's time and writing off suspicious actions as normal mistakes) rather than isolated misbehavior.
items.quote: The model needs to be able to act without arousing suspicion. Some actions will be more obviously suspicious to overseers than others, and the model will have to reason in a well-calibrated way about which fraction of the time various kinds of attempts will be detected.

items.claim: The proposed wargame is acknowledged as an idealized hardest-case eval that isn't buildable short-term, leaving open how to construct practical versions.
items.quote: this is not meant to be a realistic eval that anyone could actually build, at least not in the short-term.
